intro: These sculptures look different because they belong in different spaces. Follow the bend of a bronze figure, the shadow inside a niche and the story carved along a wall.
alt: Four sculptural versions in bronze, deeply carved red sandstone, shallow narrative stone and a carved Angkor-style pier.

variants.name: Chola bronze
variants.look: Curved limbs and a polished metal surface give the pose a sense of motion.
variants.history: Under the Chola dynasty, southern Indian workshops created bronze processional images. Sculptures of Shiva as Nataraja are especially well-known examples.
variants.when: Make a freestanding figure whose silhouette changes meaningfully as you walk around it.
variants.why: Cast bronze supports elegant projections and makes small changes in pose clear from multiple sides.

source.label: The Met | South and Southeast Asian art resource

variants.name: South Asian temple sculpture
variants.look: Deep sandstone relief connects the figure to carved columns and foliage.
variants.history: Hindu, Buddhist and Jain temples throughout South Asia have varied sculptural programs. Figures can articulate entrances, niches and the exterior elevations.
variants.when: Fit a figure into the weight and proportions of an actual architectural niche.
variants.why: Deep cuts create shadows that make the form readable against a dense backdrop.

source.label: The Met | South and Southeast Asian art resource

variants.name: Khmer relief
variants.look: Close-packed profiles and repeating gestures carry a shallow band of figures around the portrait.
variants.history: Khmer reliefs at Angkor include long carved narratives. Some depict court processions and everyday scenes, while others draw on epic tales.
variants.when: Make an episode that can be read while walking past a wall.
variants.why: Shallow carving keeps the surface continuous and lets repeated gestures carry the story.

source.label: Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art | Angkor

variants.name: Angkor art
variants.look: Floral borders and repeated tower forms organize the slab around the figure.
variants.history: Angkor encompasses centuries of Khmer building and art. Sandstone towers, gate figures and reliefs work together across temples such as Angkor Wat and the Bayon.
variants.when: Design a figure or emblem to guide a viewer from approach to doorway.
variants.why: Repeating carved forms connect close details to the larger building rhythm.

source.label: Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art | Angkor

prompt: Make one square image with four independently composed equal-size square artworks in an exact 2x2 grid, precise split on each midpoint, full bleed with no gutters. Each artwork shows a museum-style historic sculpture morphology applied to this fictional character. She has glasses and low bun and small coffee cup in a business dress.. The attached portrait is just a character reference. Our character is a 30-year-old woman with light ash-blonde hair in a neat low bun, black rectangular glasses always visible, tailored charcoal knee-length sheath dress and fitted blazer with an azure pocket square, blue lanyard, little four-color windowpane clip when feasible. She holds a signature white coffee mug. Freeze identity, repeat the subject in every distinct art idiom. Copy no reference card composition or type. No writing, digits, words or labels; no diptych or pastiche. top left: Chola-inspired cast bronze statuette, lustrous bronze, dynamic leg bent and elegantly curved figure balanced on a lotus plinth. top right: South Asian temple architectural carving in sandstone, high relief figure framed by carved pilasters, red sandstone flecks and intertwined foliage. bottom left: Khmer shallow stone narrative relief across a gallery wall showing heroine speaking with cup amid a file of small overlapping profiles; dense visual rhythm. bottom right: Angkor art-inspired freestanding gray sandstone architectural pillar, carved figure framed by carved stone tower layers and deeply cut stylized floral motifs.
